questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Why are they classified as Group I elements? *[1 mark]*

(ii) Which of the elements is the least reactive? *[1 mark]*

(iii) Write the electronic configuration of potassium (K). *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Each of them has **one electron in its outer shell** (one valence electron), so they have similar chemical properties and sit in the same vertical group of the periodic table.

(ii) **Lithium.** Reactivity increases down Group I: the outer electron is further from the nucleus and better shielded, so it is lost more easily. Lithium, at the top, is the least reactive of the four.

(iii) Potassium has atomic number 19, so 19 electrons: **2, 8, 8, 1** (that is $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,4s^1$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) These elements are usually stored under paraffin. Explain.

(ii) Write an equation for the reaction between sodium and water. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Group I metals are **very reactive**: they react quickly with oxygen and with moisture in the air (they tarnish and may catch fire). Paraffin (oil) is unreactive and keeps air and water away from the metal.

(ii) Sodium reacts vigorously with cold water giving sodium hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas:

$2\mathrm{Na(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$

(Check: left 2 Na, 4 H, 2 O; right 2 Na, 2 O, 2 + 2 = 4 H. Balanced.)
themes: chemical equations of metals with water

questions.enonce_markdown:
Lithium though in Group I of the periodic table resembles magnesium in Group II in its chemical properties.

(i) What name is given to this resemblance?

(ii) State the products formed when the carbonates of Li and Na are strongly heated:

$\mathrm{Li_2CO_3}$

$\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) A **diagonal relationship** (lithium in Group I resembles magnesium, which lies diagonally below and to its right).

(ii) Lithium carbonate decomposes on strong heating, like magnesium carbonate, giving the oxide and carbon dioxide:

$\mathrm{Li_2CO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}$

Sodium carbonate is thermally stable: it does **not** decompose at the temperature of a Bunsen flame, so **no products** are formed (it only melts at very high temperature).

questions.enonce_markdown: State the type of compound formed when Group I elements combine with non-metals. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown: **Ionic (electrovalent) compounds.** Each Group I atom loses its single outer electron to form a positive ion ($\mathrm{M^+}$); the non-metal atom gains the electron to form a negative ion. The oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction, for example $\mathrm{Na^+Cl^-}$ in sodium chloride.
